body: According to the decision, Ordinary Faces LLC leased space from Bohemian Brethren Presbyterian Church to operate a preschool. To run the school it needed a letter of no objection from the city Department of Buildings. The Department denied the initial application because there was no functional fire alarm system, and the Fire Department did not sign off on an alarm until July 26, 2016, nearly two years after the lease was signed. Department of Buildings violations related to a defunct dumbwaiter shaft, issued against parts of the building outside the leased premises, also stood in the way of a permanent letter.

The preschool and its founder sued the church in New York County Supreme Court (Index No. 654614/17). After a jury trial before Justice Joel M. Cohen, judgment was entered on August 20, 2025 awarding the plaintiffs $1,216,177.36. The church appealed the judgment and several rulings, including the denial of its motion to set aside the verdict and of its motion to strike the jury demand.

The First Department found the evidence sufficient. It held that the church breached section 18(a) of the lease, which required it to cooperate in obtaining approvals for the school, by failing to file the paperwork needed to clear the violations; the church's treasurer testified that it never had its elevator company file that paperwork. The church also breached a lease rider requiring the parties to act "expeditiously and diligently" on the fire alarm. Because the violations were issued against areas outside the leased premises, the court said curing them was the church's obligation.

The panel rejected the church's argument that a 50 percent rent abatement from January through August 2015 was the tenant's sole remedy, because the rider did not say so. It upheld the $734,353 lost-profits award, which the plaintiffs said approximates two and a half years of projected profits, noting that the figures were based on data from a preschool that had operated in the same space for nearly 40 years, which the founder testified the church provided, and that the church offered no contrary evidence. It held that section 19 of the lease, limiting the tenant to the landlord's interest in the building, allowed recovery from the proceeds of the church's 2019 sale. It also upheld the finding that the church waived the lease's jury waiver by raising it four months after the note of issue, and declined to order a new trial over brief, unsolicited testimony about the founder's personal history, to which the church did not object at trial.

timeline.label: Tenant begins receiving a 50 percent rent abatement, which runs through August 2015
Fire Department signs off on the fire alarm system, nearly two years after the lease was signed
Preschool and its founder sue the church in New York County Supreme Court (Index No. 654614/17)
Judgment entered on jury verdict awarding $1,216,177.36
Appellate Division, First Department unanimously affirms
